fatal_errors: The hypothesis changes the material from as-cast FCC+B2 AlCoCrFeNi2.1 to unspecified single-phase BCC refractory HEAs.
It replaces controlled intermediate-temperature aging with an ill-defined attempt to introduce edge dislocations by deformation.
It addresses yield-strength retention rather than the target ductile-brittle-ductile toughness transition.
It omits L12 ordering, antiphase-boundary energy, planar slip, jagged B2/FCC phase boundaries, and ductile phase-boundary transition zones.
The asserted 10-20% strengthening, 500 MPa baseline, and temperature/stress boundaries are not supported by the cited evidence.
The evidence supports edge-dislocation-controlled high-temperature strength in particular BCC HEAs, not increased toughness caused by adding edge dislocations.
The proposed tensile test does not verify that edge dislocation character was selectively changed and therefore cannot isolate the claimed mechanism.
explanation: The response is only broadly aligned with the topic of mechanical behavior in HEAs. It does not reconstruct the target system, thermal-aging intervention, brittle temperature window, structural mediators, or non-monotonic ductility outcome. E1 and E3 validly indicate that edge dislocations can govern strength retention in specific BCC refractory HEAs, but they do not establish that deliberately increasing edge-dislocation density raises toughness; deformation may instead alter total dislocation density, work hardening, residual stress, and damage simultaneously. E2 concerns phase stability and strength-ductility design rather than the proposed edge-dislocation intervention. Although the response supplies nominal bounds and a falsification threshold, these are arbitrary, and the experiment lacks dislocation-character measurements needed to discriminate the mechanism.
